messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 68
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: School Counselor
  trauma_type: Assault
  pcl5: 62

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell, Emotional Closeness: Someone getting emotionally close to me, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Dissociate Deliberately: deliberately try to leave my body or blank out, Avoid People: avoid other people, Avoid Intimacy: Being emotionally close or intimate with others
  Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Snapshot Memory: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind., Sudden Pieces: Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Gerald Whitmore is a 68-year-old married school counselor who presented for an initial psychological assessment following a referral from his primary care physician. He is soft-spoken and deliberate in his speech, choosing his words carefully — a habit that, in the counseling office where he has spent three decades helping adolescents, has always served him well. In recent months, however, that careful composure has begun to cost him considerably more effort than it once did.

Approximately fourteen months ago, Gerald was assaulted in the parking garage beneath the community center where he volunteers on weekend evenings. A man he did not recognize approached him from behind, smelling strongly of alcohol, and attacked him without warning or apparent provocation. What followed lasted only minutes, but Gerald describes those minutes as a series of frozen images: the concrete pillar his face was pressed against, the yellow fluorescent light flickering overhead, the feeling of his own breath leaving him. He was found by a passerby, transported by ambulance, and treated for a fractured orbital socket and two broken ribs. The hospital corridor where he was stabilized — bright, antiseptic, humming with clinical urgency — was the last environment he was fully conscious of before he lost track of time.

In the weeks after the assault, Gerald returned to work as quickly as his physician permitted. He told his wife, Donna, that staying busy was the only sensible thing to do. But something had already begun to shift. When he remembered the event — and he found that he did, without choosing to — it did not feel like remembering. The terror he had felt in that parking garage arrived again whole, as if the interval between then and now had collapsed entirely. The memory did not come as a narrative but as a sequence of snapshots, each one vivid and self-contained: the smell of alcohol on the man's breath, the flicker of that light, the cold of the floor. Fragments of these images surfaced without warning during ordinary moments — while reviewing a student's file, while eating dinner — and then receded just as abruptly, leaving Gerald disoriented and ashamed.

He had come to believe that if he could keep enough distance between himself and the world around him, these intrusions might lose their grip. He began arriving at work earlier and leaving later, structuring his day to minimize unplanned encounters in the hallways. When students came to him in emotional distress — which, in his role, they did regularly — he found himself doing something he could not entirely account for: a kind of internal retreat, a deliberate effort to go somewhere else inside himself, to blank out just enough that their anguish did not reach him. He was certain this made him a worse counselor, and the certainty troubled him deeply, but the alternative felt untenable.

At home, the distance had widened in ways Donna had begun to name. Gerald had always been a physically affectionate husband; he was no longer. When she reached for him — not with desire, simply with the ordinary tenderness of a long marriage — he found himself withdrawing before he understood why. What frightened him most was not the withdrawal itself but his inability to explain it to her in terms that made sense, because it did not fully make sense to him. He knew only that closeness, emotional proximity of any kind, had come to feel like exposure to something he could not manage.

The smell of antiseptic became its own problem. Gerald accompanies students to the school nurse's office several times a week, and the sharp, clinical scent of that small room had begun to stop him at the threshold in a way he could not disguise indefinitely. A colleague noticed. Gerald said he had a headache. He said it again the following week.

It was Donna who finally asked him directly whether he had spoken to anyone about what had happened in that garage. He told her he was fine. Two weeks later, he made the appointment. He came to the first session holding his hands very still in his lap, and what he said he most hoped for was to be able to sit with a student who was crying without feeling the need to disappear.
